enfranchise

/en-FRAN-chyz/ - the stress falls on FRAN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Enfranchise means to grant the right to vote.

The island's new constitution enfranchised every resident over sixteen, and the first election tripled the turnout.

Example

For sixty years the festival's best-picture prize was chosen by critics alone; last spring the board enfranchised the audience, handing every ticket holder a ballot and a stubby pencil on the way in.

Enfranchise is precise: it grants the franchise — the vote itself. Empowering a group can mean anything from funding to flattery; enfranchising them puts a ballot in their hands. Centuries ago the word also covered freeing slaves and chartering towns, but the ballot sense is the one exams love.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

empower: To empower a group is to hand it power of any kind — funding, authority, confidence, a seat at the table. Enfranchise grants exactly one power: the vote itself. Every act that can enfranchise people also empowers them, but only the ballot makes the word enfranchise correct.

naturalize: To naturalize an immigrant is to make them a legal citizen of their new country — often the step taken just before a state will enfranchise them. Citizenship and the vote travel together but are not the same grant: papers first, then the ballot.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disenfranchise: to strip the vote away — the word survives mostly in this negative twin

silence: to shut a voice out of decisions, formally or not

Where it sits · how binding the group's say is — poll → consult → enfranchise

poll vs. enfranchise: To poll a group is only to ask what it thinks — the answers bind no one; it stops far short of enfranchise.

consult vs. enfranchise: Consult goes further than poll but stops short of enfranchise: a consulted group is heard; an enfranchised one casts votes that must be counted.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-

Prefix — en-: in; cause to be

Root — franch

Root — franch: free - Old French franc

Suffix — -ise

Suffix — -ise: verb ending

Put it together

Put it together: En- (cause to be) + franc (free) + -ise = to make free. In the Middle Ages a franchise was a freedom granted from above — to hold a market, to run a town, to vote — and enfranchising someone admitted them to it. The ballot sense won out: to enfranchise is to free a voice into the voting booth.

Use the root in a new word: frank

Use the root in a new word: frank: Be frank with me, the coach said — frank means speaking as a free person does, holding nothing back.

Word Building

Word Choice

civic / historical

Enfranchise whenever the thing granted is the vote — constitutions, referendums, reform acts. Its unit-mate entitle grants a right of any kind: a refund, a discount, a tour. Enfranchise grants exactly one right, and its shadow, disenfranchise, takes that right away.
